Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) execution method

Source: R/fft.R
fft_method.Rd

Configures the binned-convolution backend for analog_search() and its wrappers. For kernel-weighted summary stats (regression, density, impact, etc.), the FFT method computes an approximate result without visiting every focal-analog pair, which can make it orders of magnitude faster for large problems. Use this function by passing the result as method = fft_method(...), or use method = "fft" for the defaults.

Usage

fft_method(bin = 0.25, check = 0, max_cells = 1e+08)

Arguments

bin

Grid spacing, as a fraction of each kernel's scale: theta for Gaussian and inverse kernels, max for uniform kernels (see Details). Default 0.25.

check

Number of randomly chosen focals to recompute with the exact engine for an accuracy report, attached to the output as the fft_check attribute (see metadata()). Default 0 (no check).

max_cells

Upper limit on the number of grid nodes, as a guard against memory exhaustion (each node of each grid takes 8 bytes). Default 1e8.

Value

An object of class "analog_fft_method".

Details

How it works

FFT is only compatible with kernel-weighted summary statistics. Rather than separately visiting every focal-analog pair, as in the "exact" method, FFT (a multivariate version of binned kernel estimation; Wand 1994) evaluates them for all focals at once using an coarse internal grid. Nodes are spaced at a fraction (bin) of each kernel's bandwidth. Each sum (or related value liek regression coefficient) is then computed in three steps:

  1. Bin. Each pool point's contribution is split among the grid nodes surrounding it, in proportion to its closeness to each (linear binning). The grid then holds how much pool "mass" lies near each node.

  2. Convolve. Each node is assigned the kernel-weighted sum of the mass at every node, done via the fast Fourier transform by transforming the grid and the kernel, multiplying them, and transforming back. The grid is padded by one kernel width of empty nodes along each axis, so that mass near one edge does not wrap around to the opposite edge.

  3. Read off. Each focal's value is interpolated from the grid nodes surrounding its exact location and environment (multilinear interpolation).

Because the convolved surface is a sum of kernel-shaped bumps, it changes little between nodes spaced well within the kernel's width, so the coarse grid loses little accuracy. The output keeps the resolution of the focal data: two neighboring focal raster cells with different climates read off different parts of the environmental axes and can get quite different results. Statistics that need several sums (for example, a regression needs weighted cross-products of the covariates and y) repeat the bin and convolve steps once per sum. For leave-one-out (exclude_self = TRUE), each focal's own binned contribution is subtracted after read-off.

The grid covers only the region where focals and pool points are within each other's reach, so focals confined to part of the pool's extent cost less. A family's nodes are spaced at bin * theta (bin * max for a uniform kernel, or bin * min if a geographic min is smaller than theta), shrunk slightly so that nodes fall exactly on the ends of the range.

Accuracy and cost

bin controls the trade-off between accuracy and cost. For the Gaussian kernel, binning error shrinks with the square of bin; for the inverse kernel (which has a sharp peak at zero distance) and for hard edges (uniform kernels, max/min cutoffs where the weight is still appreciable, count) it shrinks roughly in proportion to bin. Hard limits are anti-aliased on the grid (each node counts in proportion to the fraction of its cell inside the limit), which reduces but does not remove this edge error. Halving bin multiplies the number of grid nodes by 2^d for d active axes. The default bin = 0.25 typically gives errors well under 1%, but error at a given bin is larger in sparse neighborhoods and for ratio statistics such as regression coefficients; use check to measure it.

When to use it

The FFT method's cost is set by the size of its grid rather than by the number of focal-analog pairs. Each axis has roughly range / (bin * theta) nodes, where range is the data's extent along that axis, and grid size is the product over axes. So what matters is how many axes are active and how narrow the kernels are relative to the data's range:

  • Two active axes (e.g. two environmental variables, or a geographic kernel alone): the grid stays small even for narrow kernels, and the FFT method is typically one to three orders of magnitude faster than the exact method for large numbers of focals.

  • Three or more active axes: grid size grows with the product of the range-to-bandwidth ratios across axes. The FFT method pays off when the kernels are wide relative to the data's range. When a kernel is narrow, analog neighborhoods are small, the exact method's search index is efficient, and the FFT grid may exceed max_cells.

Speedups also shrink with more threads, since the exact method parallelizes over focals more completely than the FFT method. When in doubt, time both on a subset of focals. If max_cells is exceeded, use a coarser bin or the exact method; for raster inputs, tiled_analog_search() accepts method = "fft" and builds a separate, smaller grid for each tile and its halo (spanning only the environments found there), which is the most effective way to cut peak memory when geographic axes are active.

Requirements

Geographic kernels require projected coordinates (ideally an equal-area projection), since on a longitude/latitude grid a fixed-distance kernel changes shape with latitude. The FFT method requires select = "all" and a raw (non-index) pool, and does not support stat = "none", x_cov, downsample < 1, or design-based standard errors for "regression". Gaussian kernels without a max are truncated at 7 theta.

References

Wand, M. P. (1994). Fast computation of multivariate kernel estimators. Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics, 3(4), 433-445.

See also

analog_search()

Examples

fft_method()
#> <analog_fft_method> bin = 0.25, check = 0, max_cells = 1e+08
fft_method(bin = 0.1, check = 500)
#> <analog_fft_method> bin = 0.1, check = 500, max_cells = 1e+08
